assertion.prompt: Why does the measured origin licensing deficit in patient cells fail to predict S-phase progression rate or clinical severity?
attaches_to: pathophysiology#Delayed S-Phase Entry and Reduced Cell Proliferation
assertion.rationale: Licensing capacity is impaired in all MGORS patient cells regardless of gene, yet it does not correlate with the rate of S-phase progression, and the clinical severity gradient (ORC1 and ORC4 most severe) is not explained by licensing measurements alone. This uncoupling is a central unresolved question of MGORS pathogenesis and is what motivates the parallel non-replicative arms, notably the centriole and ciliogenesis route. Whether the non-canonical roles of these proteins, tissue-specific proliferative demand, or something else supplies the missing explanatory variable is unknown. One partial answer already exists for the ORC1 arm specifically: the BAH domain reads H4K20me2 to target ORC to origins, so BAH mutations remove a chromatin-targeting step rather than simply lowering licensing capacity. Whether an analogous upstream-targeting defect distinguishes the other severe arms has not been tested.

proposed_experiments.name: Parallel licensing, fork, cell-cycle and ciliogenesis phenotyping across an isogenic MGORS allelic series
proposed_experiments.description: Measure licensed origin density, fork speed, cell cycle length and ciliogenesis competence in parallel across an isogenic allelic series spanning the licensing module (ORC1, ORC4, CDT1) and the CMG module (CDC45, GINS2, GINS3), in a developmentally relevant proliferating cell type such as iPSC-derived chondroprogenitors, and test which measure predicts differentiation output.
proposed_experiments.decision_criterion: The measure whose variation across the allelic series best predicts chondrogenic differentiation output identifies the rate-limiting step.
supporting_outcome: Ciliogenesis competence predicts differentiation output better than licensed origin density, supporting the non-replicative arm as the severity determinant
refuting_outcome: Licensed origin density predicts differentiation output linearly, restoring the simple licensing-deficit model

selected_evidence.snippet: Thus, the replicative capacity in MGS patient cells does not correlate with clinical manifestation.

assertion.prompt: Why do roughly a third of endocrinologically assessed individuals with MGORS show a decreased response to growth hormone stimulation testing, when the growth failure of the syndrome is largely growth-hormone independent?
attaches_to: phenotypes#Decreased response to growth hormone stimulation test
assertion.rationale: Growth hormone therapy is ineffective in most individuals and growth velocity normalizes spontaneously after the first year of life, which points to a cell-intrinsic, GH-independent growth deficit. Yet 35.3% of endocrinologically assessed cases in a review selected for endocrinopathy or hormonal therapy had reported growth hormone deficiency, and 42.9% had low IGF-1. The abstract does not give feature-specific denominators. No study has established how a replication-initiation defect would produce a pituitary secretory abnormality - candidate routes include reduced somatotroph progenitor expansion during pituitary development and ascertainment bias in an endocrine-referred case literature - so this phenotype is deliberately left without a causal edge from the growth-restriction node rather than wired through an unsupported intermediate.

proposed_experiments.name: Systematic pituitary imaging and GH-axis phenotyping in molecularly confirmed MGORS
proposed_experiments.description: In a molecularly confirmed MGORS cohort unselected for endocrine referral, combine pituitary MRI volumetry with standardized GH stimulation testing, IGF-1 measurement and overnight spontaneous GH secretion profiling, stratified by gene arm.
proposed_experiments.decision_criterion: Reduced pituitary volume co-segregating with abnormal stimulation responses would support a developmental somatotroph deficit; normal imaging and secretion in an unselected cohort would attribute the reported GHD rate to ascertainment bias.
supporting_outcome: Pituitary hypoplasia and blunted stimulated GH secretion cluster in the same individuals and gene arms
refuting_outcome: Unselected cohort shows normal GH-axis measures, reclassifying the reported GHD rate as referral bias

selected_evidence.snippet: Growth hormone treatment is ineffective in most patients with MGS, but may be effective in patients in whom growth continues to decrease after the first year of life (usually growth velocity normalizes after the first year) and with low levels of IGF1.

assertion.prompt: How do MGORS replication defects alter alveolar development?
assertion.rationale: The clinical and genotype-phenotype evidence establishes emphysema, but neither disproportionate tissue growth nor cartilage chondroinduction identifies an alveolar mechanism. Co-occurrence with airway malacia does not establish a causal route to either finding.

assertion.prompt: What determines the tissue selectivity of MGORS, so that external ear cartilage, the patella, mammary tissue and the external genitalia are affected out of proportion to overall stature?
attaches_to: pathophysiology#Reduced Hedgehog Signaling and Impaired Chondroinduction
assertion.rationale: A uniform, cell-autonomous replication deficit should scale all tissues together, yet the phenotype is strikingly selective, and it is that selectivity, not the short stature, that makes MGORS clinically recognizable. Candidate explanations include narrow developmental windows of unusually intense proliferation in these structures and the ciliary Hedgehog and chondroinduction arm, but no cell-type-resolved human data exist.

proposed_experiments.name: Cell-type-resolved mapping of proliferative demand in MGORS-vulnerable human embryonic structures
proposed_experiments.description: Build a cell-type-resolved map of proliferative demand and replication stress in human embryonic auricular cartilage, patellar anlage and mammary bud, and test whether a licensing-deficient background preferentially depletes progenitors in exactly those compartments.
proposed_experiments.decision_criterion: Preferential progenitor depletion in the MGORS-vulnerable compartments relative to matched control compartments supports proliferative demand as the selectivity mechanism.
supporting_outcome: MGORS-vulnerable compartments show the highest proliferative demand and the greatest progenitor loss under a licensing-deficient background
refuting_outcome: Progenitor loss is uniform across compartments, implicating a tissue-specific signaling requirement instead

selected_evidence.snippet: we highlight that growth is disproportionately affected in certain structures

assertion.prompt: Does the GINS3 D24 mouse model, which is embryonic lethal, faithfully represent human GINS3-related Meier-Gorlin syndrome, in which affected individuals survive?
attaches_to: pathophysiology#Global Prenatal and Postnatal Growth Restriction
assertion.rationale: Homozygous D24 mouse embryos show intrauterine growth retardation and do not survive to birth, while the seven humans reported with the corresponding hypomorphic GINS3 genotypes survive with an MGORS-like phenotype. The mouse therefore recapitulates growth restriction but overshoots on severity, so mechanistic inferences drawn from it, particularly the accelerated senescence of the derived fibroblasts, may reflect a more complete loss of function than human disease alleles produce.

proposed_experiments.name: Humanized GINS3 allelic series calibrating mouse severity against patient fibroblasts
proposed_experiments.description: Generate a mouse allelic series carrying the specific human GINS3 hypomorphic substitutions at matched residues, and compare residual protein level, fork progression and senescence markers against patient-derived fibroblasts to calibrate where the human alleles sit on the murine severity curve.
proposed_experiments.decision_criterion: Concordance of residual protein level, fork speed and senescence markers between the humanized mice and patient fibroblasts establishes the translational validity of the murine readouts.
supporting_outcome: Humanized alleles produce viable mice whose fibroblast phenotypes match patient cells, validating the model
refuting_outcome: Humanized alleles remain lethal or produce senescence far exceeding patient cells, confining the model to loss-of-function extremes

selected_evidence.snippet: We further showed that mouse embryos homozygous for a D24 variant presented intrauterine growth retardation and did not survive to birth

assertion.rationale: Clitoromegaly with hypoplastic labia is reported in the endocrine-selected case literature despite normal reported gonadal hormones. assertion.rationale: The clinical review documents the three airway sites as a combined 10/24 frequency but does not identify the airway cell type or developmental process responsible. The existing chondroinduction experiments address ciliary signaling in cell models; they do not establish an airway-specific route in patients. These findings remain without causal in-edges.

assertion.prompt: What accounts for contractures, knee hyperextension, hypermobility and flat feet in MGORS?
assertion.rationale: Contractures including club feet are documented in 7/30 assessed cases. The clinical review does not establish that they are caused by the patellar-growth defect or the cell-model chondroinduction abnormality. Joint developmental mechanisms remain unassigned rather than inferred from co-occurrence with other skeletal findings. Genu recurvatum, joint hypermobility and pes planus are also clinically described but their individual causes are not resolved; these findings are not assumed to share a mechanism.

club feet, were present in 23 % (7/30) of patients.

assertion.prompt: Does neoadjuvant denosumab increase the risk of local recurrence after subsequent curettage, and if so, is that an artefact of indication bias or a real consequence of leaving mutant stroma in a drug-induced quiescent state?
assertion.rationale: The mechanism predicts the problem. Denosumab acts on RANKL, depleting the reactive osteoclast compartment; in cell-line work it neither inhibits the growth of nor kills the neoplastic stromal cells, and it does not alter their RANKL or OPG expression. The compartment that carries the driver mutation is therefore untouched, and the new bone the drug induces may make residual tumor harder to identify and clear at surgery. Reported recurrence after denosumab-then-surgery ranges from 20% to 100% across a systematic review - a spread wide enough to be uninformative on its own, and one that could equally reflect indication bias, since the drug is given to the worst tumors. Resolving this needs a design that controls for baseline tumor severity, which no published study has.

selected_evidence.snippet: In contrast, denosumab only exerted a minimal inhibitory effect in one cell line and did not induce any apoptosis.

attaches_to: pathophysiology#Somatic H3-3A G34W Oncohistone Mutation in Mesenchymal Stromal Cells
assertion.prompt: Is the only naturally occurring animal counterpart of this disease driven by the same oncohistone, or does the canine tumor reach the same histology by a different molecular route?
assertion.rationale: The canine vertebral case reproduces the human tumor's architecture - osteoclastic giant cells evenly distributed among spindled mononuclear cells - and its destructive osteolysis, yet showed no nuclear reactivity with the H3.3 G34W mutation-specific antibody. Three readings are compatible with that result and they have different consequences. If the antibody, validated only in human tissue, simply fails to cross-react, the dog is a usable model of the human mechanism. If canine H3.3 differs in sequence context around codon 34, the species is uninformative about this driver. If canine giant cell tumors are genuinely driven by something else, then the shared histology is convergent, and the tumor's architecture is a general outcome of stromal-osteoclast cross-talk rather than a specific consequence of this oncohistone - which would be the most interesting result of the three, and would argue that the histology is not diagnostic of the mechanism. Nothing short of sequencing distinguishes them.

proposed_experiments.name: Targeted sequencing of H3-3A codon 34 in canine giant cell tumors
proposed_experiments.description: Sequence the H3-3A codon 34 region in a series of canine giant cell bone tumors, alongside alignment of the canine H3.3 epitope against the human sequence the antibody was raised to, to separate assay failure from true molecular divergence.

readouts.target: Somatic H3-3A G34W Oncohistone Mutation in Mesenchymal Stromal Cells
readouts.interpretation: Absence of any codon 34 change with a conserved epitope would establish genuine divergence; presence with a negative stain would establish assay failure. Direction is recorded as UNCHANGED because the informative result is the wild-type one.

attaches_to: pathophysiology#Somatic H3-3A G34W Oncohistone Mutation in Mesenchymal Stromal Cells
assertion.prompt: What inherited factor predisposes to giant cell tumor arising in Paget disease of bone, and does that subset share the H3-3A G34W driver curated for conventional sporadic GCTB?
assertion.rationale: This entry models conventional sporadic GCTB and asserts no inheritance. A distinct subset contradicts that framing at the level of the disease name, and is recorded here rather than silently dropped. Giant cell tumor arising in Paget disease clusters strongly in families, is disproportionately multifocal, favours flat bones over the long-bone epiphyses this entry describes, and carries roughly 50 percent five-year mortality against 0 to 5 percent for GCT without Paget disease. The predisposition is most plausibly inherited through Paget disease genetics rather than through anything in the mechanism graph curated here, but the retrieved literature does not establish the germline basis of the GCT phenotype specifically, and does not report whether these tumors carry H3-3A G34W at all. Until that is known it is not possible to say whether PDB-associated GCT is the same disease arising on a permissive background, or a mechanistically separate entity sharing a histological name - which is why it is scoped out of this entry rather than merged into it, and why a separate entry would be the right home for it.

attaches_to: pathophysiology#Somatic H3-3A G34W Oncohistone Mutation in Mesenchymal Stromal Cells
assertion.prompt: Does the H3.3-G34W oncohistone initiate a giant cell tumor in vivo, and does the stromal-to-osteoclast paracrine loop operate as modeled when both compartments are present in a living skeleton?
assertion.rationale: Every mechanistic step curated in this entry between the mutation and the osteoclast compartment - the epigenetic reprogramming, the differentiation block, SCUBE3 de-repression, the SEMA4D return signal - rests on patient-derived cultures, edited tumor-derived cell lines, and monocyte co-cultures. No genetically engineered animal carrying a knock-in G34W allele was identified in this curation pass. That matters more here than in most diseases, because the central claim is specifically about cross-talk between two cell compartments: a monoculture cannot test it, and a co-culture reconstitutes it only in the absence of bone matrix, vasculature, and an intact recruitment step. The tumor-formation experiment that establishes necessity was performed in cells that were already tumor-derived, so initiation from a normal mesenchymal progenitor remains untested.

value.prompt: Is the only naturally occurring animal counterpart of this disease driven by the same oncohistone, or does the canine tumor reach the same histology by a different molecular route?
value.rationale: The canine vertebral case reproduces the human tumor's architecture - osteoclastic giant cells evenly distributed among spindled mononuclear cells - and its destructive osteolysis, yet showed no nuclear reactivity with the H3.3 G34W mutation-specific antibody. Three readings are compatible with that result and they have different consequences. If the antibody, validated only in human tissue, simply fails to cross-react, the dog is a usable model of the human mechanism. If canine H3.3 differs in sequence context around codon 34, the species is uninformative about this driver. If canine giant cell tumors are genuinely driven by something else, then the shared histology is convergent, and the tumor's architecture is a general outcome of stromal-osteoclast cross-talk rather than a specific consequence of this oncohistone - which would be the most interesting result of the three, and would argue that the histology is not diagnostic of the mechanism. Nothing short of sequencing distinguishes them.

assertion.prompt: Does neoadjuvant denosumab increase the risk of local recurrence after subsequent curettage, and if so, is that an artefact of indication bias or a real consequence of leaving mutant stroma in a drug-induced quiescent state?
assertion.rationale: The mechanism predicts the problem. Denosumab acts on RANKL, depleting the reactive osteoclast compartment; in cell-line work it neither inhibits the growth of nor kills the neoplastic stromal cells, and it does not alter their RANKL or OPG expression. The compartment that carries the driver mutation is therefore untouched, and the new bone the drug induces may make residual tumor harder to identify and clear at surgery. Reported recurrence after denosumab-then-surgery ranges from 20% to 100% across a systematic review - a spread wide enough to be uninformative on its own, and one that could equally reflect indication bias, since the drug is given to the worst tumors. Resolving this needs a design that controls for baseline tumor severity, which no published study has.

assertion.prompt: If NS6 is caused by gain-of-function NRAS alleles that raise RAS-MAPK flux, why do 1p13.2 microdeletions that remove one NRAS copy produce an overlapping Noonan phenotype?
assertion.rationale: The canonical MAPK interpretation of NS6 involves increased signal throughput into RAF-MEK-ERK. A loss-of-dosage lesion converging on a similar clinical picture challenges a simple monotonic MAPK model; it does not establish equivalence across the parallel effector responses, including AKT. Three readings are open and the published data do not separate them: the deletion phenotype may be driven by other genes in the deleted segment rather than by NRAS; reduced N-Ras may perturb pathway output non-monotonically, so that both raising and lowering it degrades developmental signalling; or the shared features may be non-specific enough that clinical overlap does not imply mechanistic convergence. The same loss-and-gain pattern is reported for MAP2K2 and SHOC2, so this is a recurring question about RAS-MAPK dosage rather than an NRAS curiosity. Resolving it bears on whether MEK inhibition is a rational therapy for the deletion phenotype, where it could plausibly make matters worse.

proposed_experiments.description: Compare ERK pathway output and developmental phenotype across an allelic dosage series - NRAS null/heterozygous-null, wild type, and a knock-in non-hotspot NS6 allele - in one system, to test whether pathway output responds non-monotonically to N-Ras dosage or whether the deletion phenotype is carried by neighbouring genes.

assertion.prompt: Which NRAS-specific developmental mechanisms generate the remaining anatomical and cutaneous findings?
assertion.rationale: The reviewed sources establish the clinical findings but do not assign distinct tissue mechanisms to these endpoints. The zebrafish craniofacial evidence supports widening, not every facial feature; the NrasG12D mouse demonstrates ventricular septation and pulmonary valve defects, not a ductal mechanism; the atrial septal pathway link is instead a qualified extrapolation from the RASopathy review. assertion.prompt: If NS6 is caused by gain-of-function NRAS alleles that raise RAS-MAPK flux, why do 1p13.2 microdeletions that remove one NRAS copy produce an overlapping Noonan phenotype?
assertion.rationale: The canonical MAPK interpretation of NS6 involves increased signal throughput into RAF-MEK-ERK. A loss-of-dosage lesion converging on a similar clinical picture challenges a simple monotonic MAPK model; it does not establish equivalence across the parallel effector responses, including AKT. Three readings are open and the published data do not separate them: the deletion phenotype may be driven by other genes in the deleted segment rather than by NRAS; reduced N-Ras may perturb pathway output non-monotonically, so that both raising and lowering it degrades developmental signalling; or the shared features may be non-specific enough that clinical overlap does not imply mechanistic convergence. The same loss-and-gain pattern is reported for MAP2K2 and SHOC2, so this is a recurring question about RAS-MAPK dosage rather than an NRAS curiosity. Resolving it bears on whether MEK inhibition is a rational therapy for the deletion phenotype, where it could plausibly make matters worse.

assertion.prompt: Does noribogaine act as a kappa agonist or, in the elevated-dynorphin state of opioid withdrawal, as a functional antagonist, and is that difference what reconciles a kappa-agonist mechanism with an antidepressant clinical effect?
assertion.rationale: The kappa model proposes an agonist to relieve the state whose validated treatment is kappa antagonism, and ibogaine's reported antidepressant effect deepens the mismatch. The reconciliation is that noribogaine inhibits dynorphin-driven beta-arrestin recruitment more potently than it stimulates G-protein signalling, so in a high-dynorphin state it may behave as a normalizer rather than an agonist. Every measurement supporting that reading was made in heterologous systems under basal conditions, so the state-dependence the reconciliation requires has never been observed. Separately, a nonhuman-primate comparison of two biased kappa agonists attributed their milder profile to factors other than G-protein bias, which weakens the explanatory device the model leans on hardest.

proposed_experiments.name: State-dependent kappa signalling and behaviour under high dynorphin tone
proposed_experiments.description: Measure noribogaine's kappa signalling under basal and elevated dynorphin tone in the same preparation, then test whether the direction of its behavioural effect follows. In vitro, compare G-protein and beta-arrestin responses with and without a dynorphin background across the concentration range achievable in brain. In vivo, compare noribogaine's effect on intracranial self-stimulation thresholds and on conditioned place preference in opioid-naive animals against animals in spontaneous or precipitated withdrawal, where dynorphin tone is elevated.

experiment_type.preferred_term: state-dependent receptor signalling and behavioural comparison

perturbations.name: Noribogaine under basal versus elevated dynorphin tone
perturbations.description: The same compound and concentration range applied in two states, which is the comparison the normalization reading requires and that no existing study makes.

controls.name: Reference kappa agonist and reference kappa antagonist arms
controls.description: A conventional agonist and norbinaltorphimine, run in both states, to place noribogaine on a scale rather than describing it in isolation.

readouts.name: Direction of effect on reward threshold in each state
readouts.interpretation: A reversal of direction between the naive and withdrawal states is the signature of state-dependent normalization; the same direction in both states means noribogaine is simply an agonist.

proposed_experiments.decision_criterion: Direction of effect reversing between basal and high-dynorphin states supports rewriting the hypothesis as kappa-signalling normalization rather than kappa agonism. A pro-dysphoric effect in both states means the hypothesis is running in the wrong pharmacological direction and should be demoted.
supporting_outcome: Noribogaine lowers reward thresholds under elevated dynorphin tone while producing conventional kappa-agonist effects in naive animals.
refuting_outcome: Noribogaine is pro-dysphoric in both states.

assertion.prompt: Why do rodent models and uncontrolled human series report large anti-opioid effects for iboga alkaloids while the one randomized trial in opioid-dependent patients found non-significant reductions in withdrawal?
attaches_to: pathophysiology#Noradrenergic Hyperactivity and Opioid Withdrawal Syndrome
assertion.rationale: The evidence supporting every mechanism here is rodent self-administration and uncontrolled human observation, and both are prone to the same inflation. Within the preclinical corpus itself the effect is not uniform: a systematic scoping review found seven of forty studies showed no improvement over controls, three of them on ibogaine. On the human side, the randomized comparison that does exist gave noribogaine to opioid-dependent patients and produced dose-dependent QTc prolongation with withdrawal reductions that did not reach significance. The mechanistic hypotheses are being fitted to an effect whose size in controlled human testing is not established, and the strongest recent preclinical result was obtained in male rats only. This is a translational-validity gap rather than an absence of evidence, which is why it is recorded as a model mismatch.

proposed_experiments.name: Multi-site blinded replication of the iboga anti-opioid effect with both sexes
proposed_experiments.description: Run a preregistered, blinded, multi-laboratory replication of single-dose iboga alkaloid effects on opioid self-administration and reinstatement, with randomization, adequate power, both sexes, and a common protocol. Report effect sizes rather than significance, and treat the published null studies as prior observations to be reconciled rather than excluded. The purpose is to establish the size of the effect the mechanistic hypotheses are competing to explain, before further mechanism studies are designed around it.

controls.name: Blinded vehicle arm at every site
controls.description: Blinding is the specific missing control, since the reported effects come from unblinded rodent work and uncontrolled human series.

controls.name: Female cohorts at every site
controls.description: The strongest recent preclinical result was obtained in male rats only, and the metabolite's bioavailability differs by sex in rodents.

readouts.name: Effect size of the durable reduction in opioid intake
readouts.target: pathophysiology#Compulsive Opioid Seeking and Loss of Control
readouts.interpretation: A pooled effect size, with its heterogeneity across sites and sexes, replaces the current position in which single-laboratory results and published nulls sit side by side unreconciled.

proposed_experiments.decision_criterion: A replicable effect of stated size establishes the phenomenon the mechanistic hypotheses must explain and calibrates how much mechanism each needs to account for. Heterogeneity that tracks sex, strain or site relocates the question from mechanism to moderator.

assertion.prompt: Which of the three candidate mechanisms for ibogaine's anti-opioid effect is actually necessary for it, given that no study has ever infused ibogaine itself into a candidate site, or blocked a candidate receptor, while measuring opioid self-administration?
attaches_to: pathophysiology#VTA Disinhibition and Mesolimbic Dopamine Release
pathophysiology#Compulsive Opioid Seeking and Loss of Control
assertion.rationale: Three mechanisms compete to explain the same phenotype, and each rests on a different molecule or a different reinforcer. The GDNF route has a sufficiency-and-necessity pair, but for ethanol. The habenular route has a site dissociation, but for the congener 18-MC, which does not share ibogaine's neurotrophic actions. The kappa route has sufficiency from engineered analogues, not necessity for the parent drug. Ibogaine itself has never been microinjected into any site with an opioid reinforcer, and the only reported loss-of-function test against ibogaine is a partial reversal by a kappa antagonist combined with an NMDA agonist, reported once by the originating laboratory without isolating either action. Because all three routes converge on the same behavioural endpoint, demonstrating sufficiency for any one of them cannot establish that ibogaine works through it.

proposed_experiments.name: Intracerebral ibogaine site dissociation against opioid self-administration
proposed_experiments.description: Run the He 2005 and Glick 2006 designs on the parent drug rather than on a surrogate. Rats acquiring intravenous heroin or fentanyl self-administration receive ibogaine (or noribogaine) microinjected into the ventral tegmental area, the medial habenula, or the interpeduncular nucleus, with a sucrose or food arm run in parallel to test reinforcer selectivity. Measure intake acutely and at 24 hours and one week to separate the acute effect from the aftereffect, since the aftereffect is the property all three hypotheses were built to explain.

experiment_type.preferred_term: intracerebral microinjection and operant self-administration experiment

perturbations.name: Intra-VTA ibogaine microinjection
perturbations.target: pathophysiology#VTA Disinhibition and Mesolimbic Dopamine Release
perturbations.description: Site arm testing the neurotrophic route, matching the site at which ibogaine reduces ethanol self-administration.

perturbations.name: Intra-medial-habenula or intra-interpeduncular ibogaine microinjection
perturbations.target: pathophysiology#Compulsive Opioid Seeking and Loss of Control
perturbations.description: Site arm testing the habenulo-interpeduncular route, matching the site at which 18-MC reduces morphine self-administration.

controls.name: Vehicle microinjection at each site
controls.description: Site-matched vehicle to separate cannula placement from drug effect.

controls.name: Non-drug reinforcer arm
controls.description: Sucrose or food responding under the same schedule, to distinguish a selective anti-opioid effect from general response suppression.

readouts.name: Opioid infusions earned at 24 hours and one week after microinjection
readouts.target: pathophysiology#Compulsive Opioid Seeking and Loss of Control
readouts.interpretation: The aftereffect rather than the acute effect is the discriminating measurement, because acute suppression is not reinforcer-selective.

proposed_experiments.decision_criterion: A site whose microinjection reproduces the durable reduction in opioid intake while sparing the non-drug reinforcer localizes the mechanism. If intra-VTA ibogaine suffices, the neurotrophic route carries the effect; if intra-habenular ibogaine suffices, the nicotinic route does; if neither site reproduces it, the effect is systemic or distributed and none of the three site-based models is complete as stated.
supporting_outcome: Durable, reinforcer-selective reduction in opioid intake after microinjection at one site and not the other.
refuting_outcome: No site reproduces the durable effect, or every site reproduces it non-selectively, indicating a systemic or pharmacokinetic explanation.

proposed_experiments.name: Factorial receptor and neurotrophin blockade of the ibogaine aftereffect
proposed_experiments.description: Give systemic ibogaine to rats with established heroin or fentanyl self-administration and attempt to abolish the aftereffect with each candidate mechanism blocked in turn: the long-acting kappa antagonist norbinaltorphimine or Oprk1 knockout, an intra-VTA anti-GDNF neutralizing antibody or AAV-shRNA knockdown of VTA GDNF, and an alpha3beta4 arm. Run the arms in one paradigm so their effect sizes are directly comparable rather than inferred across laboratories, reinforcers and decades.

experiment_type.preferred_term: factorial pharmacological and genetic blockade experiment

perturbations.name: Kappa-opioid receptor blockade during ibogaine treatment
perturbations.description: Norbinaltorphimine pretreatment or Oprk1 knockout.

perturbations.name: VTA GDNF blockade during ibogaine treatment
perturbations.target: pathophysiology#VTA Disinhibition and Mesolimbic Dopamine Release
perturbations.description: Intra-VTA anti-GDNF neutralizing antibody or AAV-shRNA knockdown, the design that established necessity in the ethanol experiments.

controls.name: Ibogaine plus inactive comparator
controls.description: IgG control for the antibody arm and vehicle for the antagonist arm.

controls.name: Blockade without ibogaine
controls.description: Each blocking agent alone, to establish that it does not itself alter opioid intake.

readouts.name: Magnitude of the durable reduction in opioid intake
readouts.target: pathophysiology#Compulsive Opioid Seeking and Loss of Control
readouts.interpretation: Abolition of the aftereffect by one blockade identifies the necessary mechanism; partial attenuation across several arms indicates the effect is carried by more than one route.

proposed_experiments.decision_criterion: The arm that abolishes the aftereffect identifies the necessary mechanism. If no single blockade abolishes it but two or more partially attenuate it, the polypharmacological reading is correct and no single-mechanism hypothesis should be promoted.
refuting_outcome: The aftereffect survives blockade of a mechanism its hypothesis claims is necessary.

assertion.prompt: Does the persistence of ibogaine's anti-opioid effect require an induced change in the brain, or can it be explained by continued drug exposure from sequestration in fat and conversion to a long-lived metabolite?
attaches_to: pathophysiology#Compulsive Opioid Seeking and Loss of Control
assertion.rationale: Every mechanism proposed for ibogaine's durability is pharmacodynamic, so the shared premise that a lasting change in the brain is required has never itself been tested. The competing explanation is on the record and was raised by the originating laboratory: both ibogaine and 18-MC are sequestered in fat, and long-term effects may reflect slow release and conversion to noribogaine rather than any induced remodelling. Human pharmacokinetics argue against this for the parent compound, whose clearance is rapid and CYP2D6-dependent, but noribogaine persists for days and no study has correlated the magnitude of the aftereffect with concurrent brain or plasma exposure. Until that is done, a positive result for any pharmacodynamic mechanism is confounded with continued occupancy of the same target.

proposed_experiments.name: Aftereffect magnitude against concurrent brain and plasma exposure
proposed_experiments.description: In rats with established opioid self-administration, give a single ibogaine dose and then sample brain, plasma and adipose ibogaine and noribogaine at intervals spanning the aftereffect, pairing every pharmacokinetic sample with a behavioural session in the same animals. Add two dissociating arms: a lipectomised or lean-versus-obese comparison that alters depot capacity without altering the administered dose, and a dosing regimen matched to reproduce the noribogaine concentration time-course without the parent compound.

experiment_type.preferred_term: paired pharmacokinetic and behavioural time-course experiment

perturbations.name: Single systemic ibogaine dose
perturbations.target: pathophysiology#Compulsive Opioid Seeking and Loss of Control
perturbations.description: The standard single-dose regimen whose aftereffect is the phenomenon in question.

perturbations.name: Depot capacity manipulation
perturbations.target: pathophysiology#Compulsive Opioid Seeking and Loss of Control
perturbations.description: Alteration of adipose depot capacity, holding administered dose constant, to change the predicted release profile without changing the pharmacodynamic exposure at dosing.

controls.name: Noribogaine-matched infusion without ibogaine
controls.description: Reproduces the metabolite exposure curve directly, separating sustained occupancy from anything the parent drug initiated.

readouts.name: Opioid intake at each time point paired with concurrent brain noribogaine
readouts.target: pathophysiology#Compulsive Opioid Seeking and Loss of Control
readouts.interpretation: The shape of the relation is the result: an aftereffect that tracks concurrent exposure is sustained occupancy, one that outlasts it is an induced change.

proposed_experiments.decision_criterion: If the aftereffect tracks concurrent brain noribogaine and scales with depot capacity, durability is pharmacokinetic and no induced-plasticity mechanism is required to explain it. If the aftereffect persists after exposure has fallen below target-engaging concentrations, a pharmacodynamic mechanism is required and the three competing hypotheses remain live.
supporting_outcome: Reduced opioid intake persisting after brain noribogaine falls below concentrations that engage any candidate target.
refuting_outcome: Aftereffect magnitude tracks concurrent exposure and scales with adipose depot capacity.

assertion.prompt: Does ibogaine change GDNF or BDNF in treated patients, given that the only human neurotrophin data in opioid dependence are cross-sectional baselines in which GDNF is unchanged and BDNF, not GDNF, tracks craving?
assertion.rationale: The neurotrophic hypothesis makes a human prediction it has never been asked to meet. In opiate-dependent patients, serum BDNF is elevated and correlates with heroin craving while serum GDNF is unchanged and uncorrelated. That is a negative for the GDNF-specific claim, but not a decisive one, because a cross-sectional baseline in maintenance patients does not test what the model predicts, which is a change in GDNF following a dose. Rodent ibogaine also raises BDNF broadly across nucleus accumbens, substantia nigra and prefrontal cortex, so even a positive human neurotrophin signal would need to distinguish a GDNF-specific response from a general one.

proposed_experiments.name: Serial neurotrophin response in ibogaine-treated patients
proposed_experiments.description: In a jurisdiction where ibogaine treatment is legal, collect serial plasma and where feasible cerebrospinal fluid GDNF and BDNF from patients before dosing and at intervals through twelve weeks, alongside withdrawal, craving and abstinence measures and CYP2D6 genotype. The comparison that matters is within-subject change from each patient's own baseline, which is what the existing cross-sectional study could not provide.

readouts.name: Within-subject change in GDNF from pre-dose baseline
readouts.interpretation: The model predicts a GDNF rise after dosing; an unchanged GDNF alongside a clinical response would place the burden on a non-neurotrophic mechanism.

readouts.name: Within-subject change in BDNF from pre-dose baseline
readouts.interpretation: Measured in parallel to test whether any neurotrophin response is GDNF-specific, as the model requires, or general.

proposed_experiments.decision_criterion: A GDNF rise that precedes and predicts the clinical response, and is larger than the concurrent BDNF change, supports the neurotrophic model in humans. An unchanged GDNF with a clinical response, or a BDNF-dominant response, argues that the human mechanism is not the one the rodent ethanol experiments identified.
supporting_outcome: GDNF rises from baseline after dosing and the rise predicts abstinence.
refuting_outcome: GDNF is unchanged after dosing in patients who nonetheless respond.

Because all three routes converge on the same behavioural endpoint, demonstrating sufficiency for any one of them cannot establish that ibogaine works through it.

proposed_experiments.name: Intracerebral ibogaine site dissociation against opioid self-administration
proposed_experiments.description: Run the He 2005 and Glick 2006 designs on the parent drug rather than on a surrogate. Rats acquiring intravenous heroin or fentanyl self-administration receive ibogaine (or noribogaine) microinjected into the ventral tegmental area, the medial habenula, or the interpeduncular nucleus, with a sucrose or food arm run in parallel to test reinforcer selectivity. Measure intake acutely and at 24 hours and one week to separate the acute effect from the aftereffect, since the aftereffect is the property all three hypotheses were built to explain.

experiment_type.preferred_term: intracerebral microinjection and operant self-administration experiment

perturbations.name: Intra-VTA ibogaine microinjection
perturbations.target: pathophysiology#VTA Disinhibition and Mesolimbic Dopamine Release
perturbations.description: Site arm testing the neurotrophic route, matching the site at which ibogaine reduces ethanol self-administration.

perturbations.name: Intra-medial-habenula or intra-interpeduncular ibogaine microinjection
perturbations.target: pathophysiology#Compulsive Opioid Seeking and Loss of Control
perturbations.description: Site arm testing the habenulo-interpeduncular route, matching the site at which 18-MC reduces morphine self-administration.

controls.name: Vehicle microinjection at each site
controls.description: Site-matched vehicle to separate cannula placement from drug effect.

controls.name: Non-drug reinforcer arm
controls.description: Sucrose or food responding under the same schedule, to distinguish a selective anti-opioid effect from general response suppression.

readouts.name: Opioid infusions earned at 24 hours and one week after microinjection
readouts.target: pathophysiology#Compulsive Opioid Seeking and Loss of Control
readouts.interpretation: The aftereffect rather than the acute effect is the discriminating measurement, because acute suppression is not reinforcer-selective.

proposed_experiments.decision_criterion: A site whose microinjection reproduces the durable reduction in opioid intake while sparing the non-drug reinforcer localizes the mechanism. If intra-VTA ibogaine suffices, the neurotrophic route carries the effect; if intra-habenular ibogaine suffices, the nicotinic route does; if neither site reproduces it, the effect is systemic or distributed and none of the three site-based models is complete as stated.
supporting_outcome: Durable, reinforcer-selective reduction in opioid intake after microinjection at one site and not the other.
refuting_outcome: No site reproduces the durable effect, or every site reproduces it non-selectively, indicating a systemic or pharmacokinetic explanation.

proposed_experiments.name: Factorial receptor and neurotrophin blockade of the ibogaine aftereffect
proposed_experiments.description: Give systemic ibogaine to rats with established heroin or fentanyl self-administration and attempt to abolish the aftereffect with each candidate mechanism blocked in turn: the long-acting kappa antagonist norbinaltorphimine or Oprk1 knockout, an intra-VTA anti-GDNF neutralizing antibody or AAV-shRNA knockdown of VTA GDNF, and an alpha3beta4 arm. Run the arms in one paradigm so their effect sizes are directly comparable rather than inferred across laboratories, reinforcers and decades.

perturbations.description: Norbinaltorphimine pretreatment or Oprk1 knockout.

controls.name: Ibogaine plus inactive comparator

controls.name: Blockade without ibogaine

assertion.prompt: Does the persistence of ibogaine's anti-opioid effect require an induced change in the brain, or can it be explained by continued drug exposure from sequestration in fat and conversion to a long-lived metabolite?
attaches_to: pathophysiology#Compulsive Opioid Seeking and Loss of Control
assertion.rationale: Every mechanism proposed for ibogaine's durability is pharmacodynamic, so the shared premise that a lasting change in the brain is required has never itself been tested. The competing explanation is on the record and was raised by the originating laboratory: both ibogaine and 18-MC are sequestered in fat, and long-term effects may reflect slow release and conversion to noribogaine rather than any induced remodelling. Human pharmacokinetics argue against this for the parent compound, whose clearance is rapid and CYP2D6-dependent, but noribogaine persists for days and no study has correlated the magnitude of the aftereffect with concurrent brain or plasma exposure. Until that is done, a positive result for any pharmacodynamic mechanism is confounded with continued occupancy of the same target.

proposed_experiments.name: Aftereffect magnitude against concurrent brain and plasma exposure
proposed_experiments.description: In rats with established opioid self-administration, give a single ibogaine dose and then sample brain, plasma and adipose ibogaine and noribogaine at intervals spanning the aftereffect, pairing every pharmacokinetic sample with a behavioural session in the same animals. Add two dissociating arms: a lipectomised or lean-versus-obese comparison that alters depot capacity without altering the administered dose, and a dosing regimen matched to reproduce the noribogaine concentration time-course without the parent compound.

experiment_type.preferred_term: paired pharmacokinetic and behavioural time-course experiment

perturbations.name: Single systemic ibogaine dose
perturbations.target: pathophysiology#Compulsive Opioid Seeking and Loss of Control
perturbations.description: The standard single-dose regimen whose aftereffect is the phenomenon in question.

perturbations.name: Depot capacity manipulation
perturbations.target: pathophysiology#Compulsive Opioid Seeking and Loss of Control
perturbations.description: Alteration of adipose depot capacity, holding administered dose constant, to change the predicted release profile without changing the pharmacodynamic exposure at dosing.

controls.name: Noribogaine-matched infusion without ibogaine
controls.description: Reproduces the metabolite exposure curve directly, separating sustained occupancy from anything the parent drug initiated.

readouts.name: Opioid intake at each time point paired with concurrent brain noribogaine
readouts.target: pathophysiology#Compulsive Opioid Seeking and Loss of Control
readouts.interpretation: The shape of the relation is the result: an aftereffect that tracks concurrent exposure is sustained occupancy, one that outlasts it is an induced change.

proposed_experiments.decision_criterion: If the aftereffect tracks concurrent brain noribogaine and scales with depot capacity, durability is pharmacokinetic and no induced-plasticity mechanism is required to explain it. If the aftereffect persists after exposure has fallen below target-engaging concentrations, a pharmacodynamic mechanism is required and the three competing hypotheses remain live.
supporting_outcome: Reduced opioid intake persisting after brain noribogaine falls below concentrations that engage any candidate target.
refuting_outcome: Aftereffect magnitude tracks concurrent exposure and scales with adipose depot capacity.

selected_evidence.snippet: Ibogaine's long-term effects may be mediated by slow release from fat tissue (where ibogaine is sequestered) and conversion to noribogaine

assertion.prompt: Does ibogaine change GDNF or BDNF in treated patients, given that the only human neurotrophin data in opioid dependence are cross-sectional baselines in which GDNF is unchanged and BDNF, not GDNF, tracks craving?
assertion.rationale: The neurotrophic hypothesis makes a human prediction it has never been asked to meet. In opiate-dependent patients, serum BDNF is elevated and correlates with heroin craving while serum GDNF is unchanged and uncorrelated. That is a negative for the GDNF-specific claim, but not a decisive one, because a cross-sectional baseline in maintenance patients does not test what the model predicts, which is a change in GDNF following a dose. Rodent ibogaine also raises BDNF broadly across nucleus accumbens, substantia nigra and prefrontal cortex, so even a positive human neurotrophin signal would need to distinguish a GDNF-specific response from a general one.

proposed_experiments.name: Serial neurotrophin response in ibogaine-treated patients
proposed_experiments.description: In a jurisdiction where ibogaine treatment is legal, collect serial plasma and where feasible cerebrospinal fluid GDNF and BDNF from patients before dosing and at intervals through twelve weeks, alongside withdrawal, craving and abstinence measures and CYP2D6 genotype. The comparison that matters is within-subject change from each patient's own baseline, which is what the existing cross-sectional study could not provide.

readouts.name: Within-subject change in GDNF from pre-dose baseline
readouts.interpretation: The model predicts a GDNF rise after dosing; an unchanged GDNF alongside a clinical response would place the burden on a non-neurotrophic mechanism.

readouts.name: Within-subject change in BDNF from pre-dose baseline
readouts.interpretation: Measured in parallel to test whether any neurotrophin response is GDNF-specific, as the model requires, or general.

proposed_experiments.decision_criterion: A GDNF rise that precedes and predicts the clinical response, and is larger than the concurrent BDNF change, supports the neurotrophic model in humans. An unchanged GDNF with a clinical response, or a BDNF-dominant response, argues that the human mechanism is not the one the rodent ethanol experiments identified.
supporting_outcome: GDNF rises from baseline after dosing and the rise predicts abstinence.
refuting_outcome: GDNF is unchanged after dosing in patients who nonetheless respond.

selected_evidence.snippet: Both doses elicited a large increase in the expression of BDNF transcripts in the NAcc, SN and PFC

assertion.prompt: What are the ADCA-DN-specific age at onset, survival, and rate of cognitive decline, as opposed to the figures derived from HSAN1E and mixed DNMT1-complex cohorts?
assertion.rationale: The most frequently quoted DNMT1 natural-history numbers (mean onset 37.7 years, average survival 53.6 years, significant cognitive deficit in 89 percent by age 45) come from a cohort of nine HSAN1E kinships comprising 45 affected subjects. In the source abstract these figures are attributed explicitly to HSAN1E, not to ADCA-DN. Because HSAN1E and ADCA-DN are discrete clinical entities with different variant positions within the same domain, these values are deliberately not recorded as ADCA-DN prevalence, progression, or prognosis in this entry. No registry-scale ADCA-DN natural history cohort exists, and no variant-specific penetrance estimate is available.

proposed_experiments.name: International DNMT1 registry stratified by targeting-sequence variant position
proposed_experiments.description: Assemble an international registry of genetically confirmed DNMT1 patients with prospective standardized assessment of ataxia scales, audiometry, polysomnography, neuropsychology, and survival, analyzed with strata defined by variant position within the targeting-sequence domain (C-terminal/exon 21 versus middle and N-terminal/exon 20) rather than by clinical label alone.
proposed_experiments.decision_criterion: Stratified onset, survival, and cognitive-decline curves that differ significantly between variant-position strata would establish ADCA-DN-specific natural history and confirm that pooled DNMT1 figures are not transferable.

selected_evidence.snippet: The average survival of HSAN1E was 53.6 years.

assertion.prompt: Is there any tractable disease-modifying strategy for ADCA-DN, given that the mechanism combines impaired maintenance methylation with potentially toxic mutant-protein species?
attaches_to: pathophysiology#Mutant DNMT1 Mislocalization and Aggresome Formation
assertion.rationale: No approved or investigational disease-modifying drug, gene therapy, RNA therapy, or epigenome-editing treatment exists for ADCA-DN, and no disease-specific interventional clinical trial has been registered. The mechanism is not a clean loss of function, so simple gene supplementation is unlikely to be sufficient and broad DNMT inhibition would be expected to be harmful. Allele-selective silencing of the mutant transcript, or pharmacological correction of mutant-protein mislocalization and aggresome formation, are the mechanistically plausible directions but neither has been attempted.

proposed_experiments.name: Allele-selective mutant DNMT1 knockdown in patient-derived induced neurons
proposed_experiments.description: In induced neurons from ADCA-DN patients carrying p.Ala570Val, p.Gly605Ala, or p.Val606Phe, apply allele-selective antisense oligonucleotides or base editing to reduce the mutant transcript while preserving the wild-type allele, then measure DNMT1 subcellular localization, aggresome burden, autophagic flux, and reversal of the patient methylome and transcriptome signature.
proposed_experiments.decision_criterion: Normalization of DNMT1 localization and of the patient methylome and transcriptome signature without loss of total maintenance methylation would support allele-selective knockdown as a therapeutic direction.

selected_evidence.snippet: Our results suggest mutations in DNMT1 result in imbalanced protein homeostasis through aggresome-induced autophagy.

assertion.prompt: Do the existing DNMT1 RFTS knock-in mice model ADCA-DN, given that they carry HSAN1E-equivalent alleles and do not develop narcolepsy, deafness, or cerebellar ataxia?
attaches_to: pathophysiology#Relief of RFTS Autoinhibition and DNMT1 Destabilization
assertion.rationale: The only published knock-in mice carry mouse equivalents of the human HSAN1E variants Y495C and D490E-P491Y, which lie in the middle or N-terminal part of the targeting-sequence domain, not the C-terminal exon-21 region that defines ADCA-DN. Since intradomain variant position is the principal determinant separating the two human phenotypes, a model built on HSAN1E alleles cannot be assumed to capture the ADCA-DN phenotype. The heterozygous mice show reduced DNMT1 protein and impaired learning and memory, but the three defining ADCA-DN features (narcolepsy, sensorineural deafness, cerebellar ataxia) have not been demonstrated. Mechanistic conclusions from these mice about RFTS destabilization and cleavage are recorded as PARTIAL support for that reason. A 2025 follow-up using RFTS-mutant mice identified aberrant DNMT1-dependent RNA m5C methylation, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial dysfunction. Its published abstract does not name the mouse RFTS allele or establish translation to classical exon-21 ADCA-DN, so that branch is likewise recorded as provisional, PARTIAL support rather than an established ADCA-DN mechanism.

proposed_experiments.name: Exon-21-allele knock-in mouse with longitudinal sleep, auditory, and cerebellar phenotyping
proposed_experiments.description: Generate heterozygous knock-in mice carrying the mouse equivalent of human DNMT1 p.Ala570Val or p.Val606Phe and phenotype them longitudinally with EEG/EMG sleep architecture and cataplexy scoring, hypothalamic hypocretin neuron counts, auditory brainstem responses and distortion-product otoacoustic emissions, rotarod and gait analysis with cerebellar histology, DNA methylome and RNA m5C profiling resolved by cell type, and mitochondrial functional assays. Run the existing HSAN1E-allele lines side by side as comparators.
proposed_experiments.decision_criterion: Emergence of sleep-onset REM intrusion, cataplexy-like attacks, elevated auditory brainstem response thresholds, and progressive cerebellar degeneration in the exon-21 line but not the HSAN1E lines would establish phenotype dependence on allele position and give the field a genuine ADCA-DN model.

selected_evidence.snippet: We generated Dnmt1-M1 and Dnmt1-M2 knock-in mouse models that are equivalent to Y495C and D490E-P491Y mutation in patients with HSAN1E, respectively.

assertion.prompt: Does ADCA-DN produce net hypermethylation of normally unmethylated regions, bidirectional change that depends on locus and cell type, or both depending on the tissue examined?
assertion.rationale: A genome-wide array on DNA from a six-affected ADCA-DN family found a shift out of the lowest and upper-intermediate methylation bins into intermediate and near-complete methylation, with 82 regionally hypermethylated loci, consistent with increased methylation of normally unmethylated promoters and CpG islands. In contrast, patient fibroblasts, iPSCs, and induced neurons showed changes whose direction depended on cell type, including ZFP57 promoter hypomethylation with increased ZFP57 expression. Neither result supports the older global-hypomethylation model, but they are not obviously reconcilable with each other, and the tissue examined differs (peripheral blood-derived DNA versus derived neural cells). Resolving this determines whether any methylation episignature could serve as a diagnostic or pharmacodynamic biomarker.

proposed_experiments.name: Matched multi-tissue methylome comparison in the same ADCA-DN carriers
proposed_experiments.description: Profile whole-genome bisulfite methylomes from peripheral blood, skin fibroblasts, and iPSC-derived neurons from the same set of ADCA-DN carriers and matched controls, using one analysis pipeline, and test whether the direction of change at shared loci is concordant across tissues or genuinely dependent on tissue.
proposed_experiments.decision_criterion: Concordant direction across tissues would indicate that the earlier discrepancy was methodological; discordant direction at shared loci would confirm a genuine dependence on cell type and rule out a single blood-based episignature.

selected_evidence.snippet: Furthermore, ZFP57, which is required to maintain gene imprinting through DNA methylation during early development, was hypomethylated in promoters and exhibited upregulated expression in patients with ADCA-DN in both iPSC and iNs.

assertion.prompt: Which cell populations actually degenerate in the ADCA-DN cerebellum and auditory system, and would that support conformance to the cerebellar_purkinje_degeneration and sensorineural_hair_cell_loss modules?
assertion.rationale: Conformance to both modules was evaluated and declined. The cerebellar_purkinje_degeneration module turns on Purkinje neuron degeneration as its central effector, but the only ADCA-DN cerebellar data are MRI atrophy and a raised MR spectroscopy myo-inositol signal, which reflects glial density rather than Purkinje loss; no autopsy series exists. The sensorineural_hair_cell_loss module turns on hair cell mechanotransduction failure and death, whereas the ADCA-DN deafness is described as sensory neuronal and is accompanied by attenuated brainstem auditory evoked potentials, which points to auditory-neural or retrocochlear rather than hair cell pathology. Declaring conformance in either case would assert an effector cell type that has not been demonstrated. Both decisions should be revisited if neuropathological or temporal-bone data appear.

proposed_experiments.name: Cerebellar and temporal-bone neuropathology in ADCA-DN donors
proposed_experiments.description: In ADCA-DN brain and temporal-bone donations, perform calbindin and parvalbumin immunohistochemistry with stereological Purkinje cell counts and Bergmann glia assessment in the cerebellar cortex, and cytocochleogram analysis of inner and outer hair cells together with spiral ganglion neuron counts in the temporal bone.
proposed_experiments.decision_criterion: Significant Purkinje cell loss relative to age-matched controls would justify conformance to cerebellar_purkinje_degeneration; a hair-cell-loss cytocochleogram pattern would justify conformance to sensorineural_hair_cell_loss, whereas isolated spiral ganglion or auditory nerve loss would confirm the retrocochlear interpretation and the decision to decline.

assertion.prompt: Is BOLD cerebrovascular reactivity to CO2 a valid surrogate for the serotonergic CO2-chemoreception deficit that links convulsive seizures to SUDEP, or does it measure cerebral vascular physiology that is mechanistically distinct from the ventilatory chemoreflex and confounded by fenfluramine's direct vasoactive pharmacology?
attaches_to: pathophysiology#Impaired CO2 Chemoreception and Postictal Hypoventilation
assertion.rationale: NCT07112365 (FAST-DS) makes cerebrovascular reactivity its primary endpoint and the hypercapnic ventilatory response only secondary, but the published mechanistic chain runs entirely through the ventilatory arm. Cerebrovascular reactivity and the hypercapnic ventilatory response are different constructs sharing only a CO2 stimulus: CVR is the cerebral vasculature dilating, HCVR is the brainstem driving breathing. A literature search finds no publication linking CVR to SUDEP risk, to CO2 chemoreception, or to fenfluramine exposure; CVR has been used in epilepsy only to localize the epileptogenic zone, a different purpose entirely. Two failure modes follow. First, a null CVR result would not refute the serotonergic chemoreflex model, because that model makes no CVR prediction. Second, and more consequential, a positive CVR result is ambiguous: fenfluramine acts at 5-HT2B receptors on non-neural tissue, the same pharmacology behind its valvulopathy and pulmonary-hypertension liability, so a drug-induced change in cerebral vascular reactivity could be direct vasoactivity with no bearing on chemoreception or SUDEP risk. The trial's own plan to relate CVR to the simultaneously measured ventilatory response is therefore the load-bearing analysis, and dismech should not promote CVR above CANDIDATE_SURROGATE until it reports.

proposed_experiments.name: Within-subject concordance of cerebrovascular and ventilatory CO2 responses
proposed_experiments.description: In the same hypercapnia session, measure BOLD cerebrovascular reactivity and the hypercapnic ventilatory response in Dravet syndrome patients and in healthy controls, before and after fenfluramine, and test whether the two co-vary within subject and whether fenfluramine moves them together or independently. Include a vasoactive control condition that changes cerebral vascular tone without changing serotonergic tone, so a CVR shift attributable to direct vasoactivity can be separated from one tracking chemoreflex gain.

assertion.prompt: Does fenfluramine reduce SUDEP risk in Dravet syndrome through a serotonergic action on postictal CO2 chemoreception that is separable from its anticonvulsant effect, or is the observed mortality reduction fully explained by having fewer generalized convulsive seizures?
attaches_to: pathophysiology#Impaired CO2 Chemoreception and Postictal Hypoventilation
assertion.rationale: This is the discriminating question between the two mechanistic hypotheses curated on this entry, sudep_seizure_burden_model (CANONICAL) and sudep_serotonergic_chemoreflex_model (EMERGING). The entire protective arm of the serotonergic model rests on model-organism pharmacology: 5-HT depletion worsens and fenfluramine rescues the postictal chemoreflex deficit in Scn1a mice, and fenfluramine blocks seizure-induced respiratory arrest in DBA/1 mice via 5-HT4 receptors. On the human side, seizures are shown to impair CO2 chemoreception in patients, but no human study has measured any effect of fenfluramine on CO2 chemoreception at all; a PubMed search for fenfluramine combined with hypercapnic ventilatory response or CO2 chemoreception returns nothing. The human SUDEP evidence is a pooled historical-control comparison resting on three deaths across 1185 person-years, sponsored by the drug's manufacturer, with no randomized SUDEP endpoint. Because fenfluramine also reduces convulsive seizure frequency, and convulsive seizure burden is itself the dominant SUDEP risk factor, that comparison cannot separate the two models. The distinction matters for curation and for practice: only under the serotonergic model does the chemoreflex become a target and a risk-stratification biomarker in its own right, and only under that model would a patient with preserved seizure control but a low chemoreflex gain still warrant attention.

Comparator arms treated with an equally effective non-serotonergic anticonvulsant provide the critical contrast: if chemoreflex gain improves only with fenfluramine at matched seizure reduction, the serotonergic arm is separable.

assertion.prompt: Does enhanced serotonergic tone protect against seizure-induced respiratory death by restoring CO2 chemoreflex gain, as this entry models it, or by facilitating autoresuscitation through the periaqueductal gray and pontomedullary respiratory nuclei without raising ventilatory drive at all?
attaches_to: pathophysiology#Impaired CO2 Chemoreception and Postictal Hypoventilation
assertion.rationale: The chemoreflex model asserts a specific locus for serotonergic protection: 5-HT tone sets the gain of the hypercapnic ventilatory response, so restoring it should restore ventilation to a CO2 load. Two model-organism results point somewhere else. Fluoxetine blocks seizure-induced respiratory arrest at doses that do not raise basal ventilation, while doxapram and PK-THPP raise ventilation and fail to protect, which is a double dissociation between the protective effect and ventilatory drive. Imaging of protected animals localizes the fluoxetine effect to the periaqueductal gray plus amygdala, reticular formation, Kolliker-Fuse nucleus, facial-parafacial group and pontine raphe, a distribution that reads as a network for recovery of breathing after an arrest rather than as chemoreceptor gain. Both experiments are in the audiogenic DBA/1 model rather than an Scn1a haploinsufficient Dravet model, and neither measured breathing during the seizure itself, so they motivate a competing locus without excluding a distinct seizure-window chemoreflex effect in Dravet. Until the two are separated, the pathophysiology chain curated here should be read as the model under test, not as the established mechanism.

Measure the hypercapnic ventilatory response, latency to resume breathing after seizure-induced apnea, and survival in each arm.

assertion.prompt: Is selective Nav1.1 loss in GABAergic, especially parvalbumin-positive, interneurons a complete account of Dravet syndrome, or do excitatory-neuron, astrocytic, and developmental contributions materially shape the phenotype?
assertion.rationale: The dominant model, grounded in Scn1a mouse work, attributes seizures to disinhibition from impaired interneuron firing with preserved excitatory pyramidal-neuron sodium current. Later single-cell, developmental, and glial data suggest the interneuron-only view may be incomplete: astrocytic calcium signalling is altered in the same model, interneuron deficits may be partly developmental and time-limited, and excitatory-neuron contributions have been proposed. For curation this means the interneuron node should remain the primary mechanism while additional cell-type and developmental contributions stay an open question rather than a settled one.

assertion.rationale: Most mechanistic and preclinical therapeutic evidence for Dravet syndrome comes from Scn1a heterozygous mice, in which seizure frequency and SUDEP are highly sensitive to strain background and in which murine sodium channel biology differs from human. assertion.prompt: Which temporal causal ordering among amyloid-beta accumulation, tau spread, microglial/astrocytic activation, mitochondrial quality-control failure, and synaptic/cognitive decline best explains stage-specific Alzheimer disease progression and cognitive resilience?
assertion.rationale: Amyloid plaques, tau tangles, glial activation, mitochondrial stress, and cognitive decline are all established Alzheimer disease features, but the disease entry should not imply a single fixed ordering across all stages. Current evidence supports amyloid-triggered tau and glial pathways, reciprocal inflammasome-to-amyloid amplification, protective TREM2-dependent microglial containment of amyloid-associated tau spread, mitochondrial quality-control effects on amyloid/tau/inflammation, and cognitive reserve that can decouple pathology burden from symptoms. assertion.prompt: Does live-attenuated herpes zoster (VZV) vaccination causally reduce dementia incidence at the population level — i.e., is the neurotropic-herpesvirus contribution to Alzheimer disease causal and preventable by vaccination — given that two regression-discontinuity analyses of the same age-based vaccine rollout reach opposite conclusions?
attaches_to: pathophysiology#HSV-1 Reactivation in RORB+ Glutamatergic Neurons
assertion.rationale: The neurotropic-herpesvirus hypothesis predicts that reducing herpesvirus reactivation (e.g., by zoster vaccination) should lower dementia risk. Multiple independent quasi-experimental studies now bear on this: three report a protective association and one eligibility-based analysis is null. On the positive side: the Welsh regression-discontinuity (RD) analysis of the date-of-birth eligibility cutoff (PMID:40175543) found that receiving the live vaccine reduced new dementia diagnoses by 3.5 percentage points over 7 years (~20% relative reduction, stronger in women); an independent Canadian analysis of natural experiments in Ontario (PMID:41579903) found that birth just before versus just after the vaccine-eligibility cutoff decreased new dementia diagnoses by 2.0 percentage points over 5.5 years, corroborated by synthetic-control comparisons against the same birth cohorts in provinces with no vaccination programme; and a vaccine-type natural experiment (DOI:10.1038/s41591-024-03201-5) found the recombinant (Shingrix) vaccine associated with even lower dementia risk than the live vaccine, again stronger in women. Against a detectable effect: an English Hospital Episode Statistics RD analysis by an overlapping author group (DOI:10.64898/2026.07.20.26358345) reproduced the expected sharp drop in hospital-coded shingles but found no detectable intention-to-treat effect of vaccine ELIGIBILITY on hospital-coded dementia, robust across specifications, placebo cutoffs, negative controls, and a separately held HES extract. A methodological reconciliation has been proposed — that the null result reflects ITT dilution by imperfect uptake plus insensitive hospital-coded ascertainment, given that dementia is largely coded in primary care and on death certificates — but it does not currently settle the disagreement, for two reasons. First, the null study tested that explanation itself: comparator analyses in Welsh data with linked primary-care and death data did not suggest its results were driven by reliance on hospital data. Second, the receipt-versus-eligibility distinction does not separate the positive studies from the null one: the Canadian headline estimate (PMID:41579903) is itself an eligibility contrast at the birth-date cutoff, like the English one, so ITT dilution alone cannot explain why the Canadian RD detects an effect where the English HES RD does not. Only the Welsh headline estimate is scaled to vaccine receipt. The designs do still differ in dementia ascertainment (primary-care records and death certificates versus hospital-coded diagnoses) and in country, health system, and follow-up length. Whether the disagreement reflects outcome ascertainment, other residual design differences, or a genuinely absent or much smaller population-level effect is unresolved — which determines how strongly the herpesvirus arm should be weighted as a causal, modifiable contributor to Alzheimer disease, and motivates a randomized controlled trial of zoster vaccination for dementia prevention.
assertion.notes: Seeded from a medRxiv paper review of DOI:10.64898/2026.07.20.26358345 (Hamilton, Geldsetzer, Davey Smith et al., 2026), then extended with a literature investigation of the wider zoster-vaccine/dementia natural-experiment landscape (Canadian Lancet Neurology RD, PMID:41579903; recombinant-vs-live vaccine-type natural experiment, Nature Medicine 2024, DOI:10.1038/s41591-024-03201-5). The residual tension is left open rather than adjudicated here: the ascertainment/dilution reconciliation is recorded as a proposed but unsettled explanation, since the null study's own Welsh comparator analyses with linked primary-care and death data did not support it, and the eligibility-versus-receipt contrast does not cleanly separate the positive studies from the null one. assertion.prompt: Which temporal causal ordering among amyloid-beta accumulation, tau spread, microglial/astrocytic activation, mitochondrial quality-control failure, and synaptic/cognitive decline best explains stage-specific Alzheimer disease progression and cognitive resilience?
assertion.rationale: Amyloid plaques, tau tangles, glial activation, mitochondrial stress, and cognitive decline are all established Alzheimer disease features, but the disease entry should not imply a single fixed ordering across all stages. Current evidence supports amyloid-triggered tau and glial pathways, reciprocal inflammasome-to-amyloid amplification, protective TREM2-dependent microglial containment of amyloid-associated tau spread, mitochondrial quality-control effects on amyloid/tau/inflammation, and cognitive reserve that can decouple pathology burden from symptoms. The open curation question is which edges are upstream drivers, downstream amplifiers, parallel state changes, or resilience modifiers in preclinical, prodromal, and dementia-stage Alzheimer disease.

assertion.prompt: By what mechanism does gluten exposure produce recurrent aphthous stomatitis, sterile inflammatory arthropathy, constipation-predominant bowel dysfunction, fatigue, and peripheral neuropathy in celiac disease, when each improves on a gluten-free diet but no intermediate step has been demonstrated in patients?
assertion.rationale: For each of these five phenotypes the association and a gluten-free-diet response are documented, but the mechanism is not, so no causal edge is recorded in the pathograph. Recurrent aphthous stomatitis: candidate routes are hematinic (iron/folate/B12) deficiency from malabsorption versus gluten-driven mucosal immune inflammation; the diet-response evidence is four adherent responders in an uncontrolled series, and nutrient correction has never been factorially separated from gluten withdrawal. Arthritis: a rigorously investigated case of sterile non-erosive polyarthritis remitted within three weeks of gluten withdrawal, and ultrasound series report more subclinical synovitis with gluten exposure, but synovial tissue has rarely been profiled and shared immune susceptibility to coincident rheumatic disease is a live alternative. Constipation: four weeks of gluten-free diet shortened small-bowel and colonic transit and increased contractility in newly diagnosed patients, yet the treatment diet itself - low in fiber and rich in refined substitutes - can cause constipation, so the phenotype can arise from the disease and from its treatment in the same patient. Fatigue: a prospective controlled study found it substantially reduced after twelve months of gluten-free diet yet still higher than in matched controls, and associated with depression and pain rather than with disease activity or nutritional deficiency - so neither the hematinic nor the inflammatory route is established and a psychosocial contribution cannot be separated out. Peripheral neuropathy: nerve biopsies show axonopathy, loss of myelinated fibers and perivascular inflammatory infiltration, which points to immune injury without settling whether the effector is humoral (anti-TG6 or antiganglioside antibodies) or cell-mediated; B12 or copper deficiency, diabetes and coincident autoimmune neuropathy also have to be excluded.

proposed_experiments.name: Blinded gluten challenge with phenotype-specific endpoints
proposed_experiments.description: In patients in remission on a gluten-free diet with a history of one of these manifestations, a randomized blinded gluten challenge with phenotype-specific endpoints (blinded ulcer counts, ultrasound synovitis scoring, wireless motility capsule transit), stratified by corrected versus uncorrected hematinic deficiency and with quantified fiber intake, to separate gluten-driven from nutritional and diet-composition routes.
supporting_outcome: The manifestation recurs or objectively worsens during blinded gluten challenge and not on placebo, independent of nutrient status and fiber intake.
refuting_outcome: No difference between gluten and placebo challenge, indicating the manifestation tracks nutrient status, diet composition, or a coincident disease rather than gluten-driven immunity.

assertion.prompt: Do the proposed amplification loops of celiac disease operate as one integrated system, and would disrupting a single loop collapse the cascade?
assertion.rationale: Three amplification loops are commonly invoked to explain why celiac disease escalates quickly and heals slowly: secretory IgA delivering gliadin peptides back across the epithelium through CD71, IFN-gamma driving thioredoxin release that reactivates extracellular TG2, and TG2-reactive B cells presenting gluten peptides to gluten-specific T cells. Each has separate experimental support, but they were characterized in different reductionist systems and have never been perturbed together in one system, so their joint contribution is an inference rather than a measurement. The follow-up cohorts that document delayed or incomplete mucosal recovery on a gluten-free diet describe the outcome without attributing it to these loops.

proposed_experiments.name: Combinatorial loop perturbation in patient-derived intestinal organoid immune co-cultures
proposed_experiments.description: In duodenal organoid or air-liquid-interface cultures retaining tissue-resident immune cells from celiac patients, block CD71-mediated retrotranscytosis, extracellular TG2 activity and B-cell antigen presentation singly and in combination during gliadin exposure, reading out gluten-specific T-cell activation, epithelial injury and anti-TG2 output.
supporting_outcome: Blocking any single loop produces a disproportionate reduction in gluten-specific T-cell activation and epithelial injury, which is the signature of a coupled amplifying system.
refuting_outcome: Single blockades produce only additive, proportionate reductions, indicating three parallel contributors rather than one nested self-amplifying circuit.

assertion.prompt: What sustains the clonal intraepithelial lymphocyte expansion of refractory celiac disease type II once it no longer depends on gluten stimulation, and at what point does the canonical model stop applying?
assertion.rationale: Refractory celiac disease type II is the clearest boundary condition on the canonical model in this entry. Dominant T-cell receptor beta clonotypes recovered from these patients are patient-specific and bear no homology to known gliadin-specific sequences, and the clones persist stably for years on a strict gluten-free diet, so the driving stimulus is no longer the antigen the rest of the entry is built around. Genetic susceptibility to the progression also appears to be separate from susceptibility to celiac disease itself. What the entry cannot yet say is what does drive the expansion, which matters because this is the pre-lymphomatous state that the gluten-free diet does not treat.
